messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Your previous vignette failed validation. Make ONLY the targeted changes listed below.

Previous vignette:
Pita is a 71-year-old married man from a Pacific Islander family who has spent the last several years working as a cashier at a neighborhood grocery store. He came to treatment after months of telling his wife he was “not right anymore,” though when pressed he struggled to say exactly what had happened. The trauma he circles around occurred outside that same store late one afternoon, when he witnessed a young mother and her baby caught in a violent assault near the entrance. He remembers the baby’s crying first, sharp and panicked, and the sudden slam of the automatic outer door as customers rushed in and out. After that, the scene breaks apart for him. He can recall flashes of people moving too fast, the mother on the ground, someone shouting for help, but whenever he tries to put the event into order he loses the thread and stops, saying there are pieces missing and that he cannot make it into a full story even in his own mind.

In the weeks afterward, the sounds and sensations that belonged to that moment began to stand out with a force he could not control. A baby crying in the store, the heavy swing of the stockroom door, even the simple discomfort of feeling hemmed in at his register could make his whole body tense before he had time to think. At work he would jerk when someone stepped suddenly into his peripheral vision, and he found himself scanning customers’ hands, faces, and movements as if danger were about to break out again. What frightened him was not only the intensity of his reaction but how quickly it took over; the cry of an infant or the crack of a door seemed to place him back inside an atmosphere where harm could happen at any second.

Those same moments also revived what he had come to believe about the aftermath. Each time the door slammed or a baby cried nearby, he was pulled back not only toward the scene but toward the bitter conviction that the people who should have protected that woman and child had failed them, and that no one had truly been held to account. He speaks with contained anger about how little seemed to happen afterward, how authorities and the systems around them did not provide the safety he had assumed existed. The triggers do not stay as mere reminders; they bring with them the meaning he has made of the event, that ordinary people are left exposed and those responsible often face nothing.

Over time Pita has become increasingly watchful. In line at the store, he studies customers for signs they may turn unpredictable. If someone reaches suddenly for a wallet or shifts a bag too quickly, he startles hard and has to steady himself against the counter. Beneath this is a settled belief that protection cannot be counted on, and that because others failed before, he has to be the one who stays on guard now. That belief keeps his attention fixed outward, always checking, always braced, as though vigilance were the only thing standing between another helpless scene and catastrophe.

His inability to form a coherent account has deepened these convictions rather than softened them. Because the memory comes in fragments, with whole sections missing, the event remains unresolved in his mind, something unfinished and uncontained. He says that if he could remember it straight through, maybe he could understand it, but instead the blanks leave him with a sense that something terrible happened in a world where no one stepped in as they should have. The more broken the memory feels, the more certain he becomes that what happened was intolerable and unforgiven; and that certainty, in turn, makes it even harder for him to stay with the memory long enough to narrate it clearly.

The fragmentation also makes his environment feel studded with warning signals. Because he cannot place the event into a complete past, babies’ cries and doors opening or slamming do not feel like neutral present-day sounds. They arrive charged, as if they contain the missing parts of what he still cannot grasp. Even a vague sense of discomfort in his body can act like a cue that something is wrong, and once cued he begins scanning the room, tracking movement and watching people closely for threat.

At home his wife has noticed how emotionally flat he has become. He sits through dinner silent, looking beyond the table, and says he feels dead inside. Yet under that numbness is an angry, mistrustful alertness that has reshaped his days. At the register he asks coworkers to handle families with crying infants when he can, and he positions himself to keep the entrance in sight. What finally brought him in was a recent incident when a child began wailing near the checkout just as the front door slammed behind a customer; Pita spun toward the sound, heart pounding, certain for a moment that someone was about to be hurt. Later he could not explain to his wife why it affected him so strongly, only that the same old certainty returned: people are not protected, no one answers for it, and he is tired of living as if danger is always one sudden movement away. He says he wants help making sense of what happened, but what he fears most is that if he stops watching, the world will prove him right again.

Issues to fix:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Negative Appraisals → Memory: The vignette does not clearly show Pita’s negative appraisals causing or intensifying the trauma memory within the same paragraph.
  e.g. "The belief that she was permanently changed kept bringing her back to the moment it had happened, as if she needed to locate exactly where she had been lost."
  e.g. "Telling herself that she should have seen it coming made the memory more vivid and easier to find — it sat there waiting, proof of her failure."
  e.g. "The conviction that she was weak fed directly into the flashback, colouring it, making it worse: she wasn't just there again, she was there again and helpless."
- Threat → Negative Appraisals: The vignette does not clearly state that his sense of threat leads to or reinforces his negative appraisals within the same paragraph.
  e.g. "The constant sense of danger was the most convincing proof she had that her life had changed beyond repair."
  e.g. "Feeling this afraid all the time, she had eventually come to accept the conclusion her body kept offering: that she was not the kind of person who got to feel safe."
  e.g. "The threat that shadowed her days quietly confirmed the thought she worked hardest to resist — that this was simply who she was now."

---

Return ONLY patch blocks — do NOT return the full vignette.

For each REQUIRED EDGE MISSING — produce one INSERT_AFTER block.
Find a paragraph in the vignette that already mentions component A, and add a sentence
after it that shows A influencing B through natural clinical language.
<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
[copy 1–2 sentences from the vignette — the anchor after which to insert]
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
[one or two sentences that convey A influencing B, written as natural clinical prose]
<<<END>>>

Output ONLY these patch blocks. No prose, no explanation, no full vignette.

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
Those same moments also revived what he had come to believe about the aftermath. Each time the door slammed or a baby cried nearby, he was pulled back not only toward the scene but toward the bitter conviction that the people who should have protected that woman and child had failed them, and that no one had truly been held to account.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
The more firmly he held that conclusion, the more insistently the scene returned in jagged images, as if his mind kept dragging him back to the mother on the ground and the crying baby to confirm that this was what the world was really like.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
Over time Pita has become increasingly watchful. In line at the store, he studies customers for signs they may turn unpredictable. If someone reaches suddenly for a wallet or shifts a bag too quickly, he startles hard and has to steady himself against the counter.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
Living in that constant state of alarm has only strengthened his belief that safety is fragile and that people in authority do not truly protect anyone; the fear itself feels like evidence that he was wrong ever to trust that they would.
<<<END>>>
